bib.title: MAUVE: Measuring the Gap Between Neural Text and Human Text using Divergence Frontiers

legacy_report:
SOURCE: MAUVE: Measuring the Gap Between Neural Text and Human Text using Divergence Frontiers. Krishna Pillutla, Swabha Swayamdipta, Rowan Zellers, John Thickstun, Sean Welleck, Yejin Choi, Zaid Harchaoui. NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv:2102.01454v3, 23 Nov 2021).

COVERAGE: Read all 119,165 of 119,165 chars across all 35 pages: main text, references (skimmed for origins), and Appendices A–G (proofs, pseudocode, package listing, setup, full result tables 6–14, human-eval protocol, cluster interpretation, example generations). Nothing skipped.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: MAUVE scores how close a model's *distribution* of text is to the human distribution. It embeds both sample sets with an external LM, quantises them together with k-means, and takes the area under a curve of soft Type I/Type II KL errors computed against mixtures R_λ = λP + (1−λ)Q.
  number: none (definition)
  setup: P = human text, Q = model + decoder. Default embedding is GPT-2 large; default quantiser is k-means with k=500.
  quote: "we jointly quantize the embedded samples (e.g. with k-means [36]), and count the cluster assignments to form histograms" / "Our proposed measure, MAUVE (P,Q ), is the area under the divergence curveC(P,Q )... MAUVE (P,Q ) lies in (0, 1], with a larger value meaning thatQ is closer toP . Further, MAUVE (P,Q ) = 1 if and only ifQ =P ."
  where: p.3–4
- claim: MAUVE rank-correlates with human pairwise judgments better than the other automatic metrics tested.
  number: 0.952 human-like, 0.810 interesting, 0.857 sensible (Spearman). Gen. PPL scored 0.810 / 0.643 / 0.738.
  setup: Web text only, GPT-2 small/medium/large/xl × {ancestral, nucleus} = 8 settings plus human text. 36 pairs × 90 ratings each, from 214 AMT workers. Completions truncated to 256 tokens and required to be at least 200 tokens. Preferences were fit with Bradley-Terry, and MAUVE was then rank-correlated against the BT scores. The correlation therefore rests on about 8 system-level points (my inference from the 8 MAUVE values in the table). Baselines were Gen. PPL, Zipf, REP, Distinct-4 and Self-BLEU. BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore against references were not tested.
  quote: "MAUVE correlates highly with human judgments of how human-like (0.952), interesting (0.810), and sensible (0.857) the machine text is... generation perplexity has correlations that are 0.12 to 0.17 lower than MAUVE ’s." / "We obtain 90 preference ratings for each pair of settings, coming from a total of 214 crowd-workers"
  where: p.9–10 (Table 5); full in Table 14, p.28
- claim: MAUVE tracks the accuracy of trained human-vs-machine discriminators and needs no training of its own.
  number: 0.956 news, 0.893 stories
  setup: News used Grover base/large/mega generations judged by a fine-tuned Grover-mega discriminator. Stories used GPT-2 medium fine-tuned on WritingPrompts, judged by a frozen GPT-2 large with a classification head.
  quote: "MAUVE correlates the highest with the discrimination accuracy (0.96 for news and 0.89 for stories) among all comparison measures."
  where: p.10
- claim: MAUVE orders decoders the expected way (greedy < ancestral < nucleus) and is not fooled by an adversarial decoder that matches human perplexity. Gen. PPL fails both tests.
  number: greedy .016, ancestral .882, nucleus .940; adversarial 0.06
  setup: Web text, GPT-2 xl, 5000 generations, max 1024 tokens.
  quote: "assigning the lowest quality to greedy decoding (.016) followed by ancestral sampling (.882), and the highest quality to nucleus sampling (.940)... generation perplexity rates the highly degenerate greedy-decoded text as better than ancestral sampling ( 11.324 vs. 19.284)"
  where: p.7 (Table 3, p.8)
- claim: MAUVE rises with model size.
  number: 0.878 / 0.915 / 0.936 / 0.940 (small→xl)
  setup: Web text, nucleus sampling.
  quote: "MAUVE (↑) 0.878 0 .915 0 .936 0.940"
  where: Table 4, p.8
- claim: MAUVE is the only metric tested that falls steadily as generations get longer. Fréchet distance improves with length, which is the wrong direction.
  number: none (Figure 4)
  setup: Web text, GPT-2 all sizes, 5 seeds.
  quote: "MAUVE is the only comparison measure which identiﬁes that generation quality decreases monotonically with increasing text length."
  where: p.7
- claim: Rankings hold up when the embedding model changes, though the absolute values move.
  number: Spearman 0.993 (GPT-2 large vs RoBERTa large)
  setup: RoBERTa was capped at 256 tokens. RoBERTa scores GPT-2 small sampling at 0.174, where GPT-2 large features give 0.589.
  quote: "The Spearman rank correlation between MAUVE computed with the two feature representations is 0.993... RoBERTa penalizes ancestral sampling more while rating greedy decoding higher"
  where: p.25 (Table 12, p.22–23)
- claim: Rankings are stable across choices of k and quantiser. The absolute value is not stable, and extreme k values make it meaningless.
  number: Spearman 0.99–1.00 for k from 100 to 5000; ≥0.99 for DRMM and lattice. Below k<100 every method scores near 1; above k>2000 every method scores near 0.
  quote: "the Spearman correlation is exactly 0.99 or 1.00" / "Ifk is too small (k <100), all methods are scored close to 1. If k is too large k > 2000), all methods are scored close to 0."
  where: p.9; p.25
- claim: Small samples inflate MAUVE and make it noisier.
  number: none (Figure 7, sample sizes 300–5000, k = n/10)
  quote: "We observe that a smaller sample size gives an optimistic estimate of MAUVE ... We also note that a smaller sample size leads to a larger variance in MAUVE ."
  where: p.25
- claim: The scaling constant c changes the value but never the ranking. The authors use c=5.
  quote: "Choice ofc does not affect the relative order of the curves but only the numerical value. We usec = 5"
  where: p.9
- claim: MAUVE is cheap to compute once embeddings exist. Self-BLEU and per-system discriminators are expensive by comparison.
  number: 1–3 minutes on one CPU core for 5000 generations; Self-BLEU takes about 7 hours
  setup: k-means variant with cached GPT-2 large hidden states, Intel i9 at 2.80GHz. DRMM takes 1.75 h; lattice takes about 5 min on a TITAN Xp.
  quote: "Computation of MAUVE usingk-means with 5000 generations takes 1− 3 minutes on a single core of an Intel i9 CPU... using cached hidden state representations from a GPT-2 large" / "This operation takes around 7 hours to compute on a single core"
  where: p.20
- claim: Reference-based n-gram metrics do not suit open-ended generation.
  quote: "classical metrics for n-gram matching [44, 32, 2]... making them fundamentally ill-suited for open-ended generation. Moreover, it has been recently shown in [ 42] show that these classical metrics only weakly agree with human judgments."
  where: p.4
- claim: MAUVE also scores beam search as degenerate.
  number: beam b=4 0.021, b=8 0.366, ancestral 0.589, nucleus 0.878
  setup: GPT-2 small, web text.
  quote: "Mauve 0.008 0 .021 0 .026 0 .366 0 .341 0 .5890.02 0.8780.007"
  where: Table 11, p.22

LIMITS
- It scores a distribution, not a single text. The inputs are lists of human and model texts ("given neural text and human text, it yields a scalar measure of the gap between them", p.1), and the paper uses 5000 per system. No per-answer score exists.
- The paper never tests factuality, faithfulness to a source, or answer correctness. The tasks are open-ended continuation of web text, news and stories, where "there is no 'correct' output; the main criteria... are coherence, creativity, and ﬂuency" (p.2). Nothing covers QA or RAG.
- The authors concede it disagrees with humans on some pairs: "MAUVE rates nucleus sampling with GPT-2 medium as being better than pure sampling from GPT-2 large and xl" (p.28). In news it preferred ancestral over nucleus for Grover large (p.23).
- Its absolute values depend on k, the embedding model, c and sample size. Only the rankings are shown to be robust, so a number like "0.9" is not comparable across setups.
- The human study rests on few points: one domain, GPT-2 models only, 256-token outputs, and AMT non-experts. The authors cite [10, 29] on human evaluations being inconsistent.
- Extending it to closed-ended tasks with references is named as future work (p.10).
- Dated: the models are 2019-era GPT-2 and Grover, and the embeddings come from GPT-2 large and RoBERTa.

BUILDS ON: information divergence frontiers, Djolonga et al. [16] (AISTATS 2020); precision-recall for generative models, Sajjadi et al. [49] (NeurIPS 2018) and Kynkäänniemi et al. [31] (NeurIPS 2019); Fréchet/FID, Heusel et al. [25] (2017); nucleus sampling and degeneration, Holtzman et al. [26] (ICLR 2020); Bradley-Terry fit following Marden [37] (1995) and Hunter [27] (2004); companion theory on estimation and quantisation error, Liu et al. [33] (NeurIPS 2021).

CODE (Listing 1, p.17; package `pip install mauve-text`; extraction inserted spaces inside identifiers, which are restored here)
```python
from mauve import compute_mauve
out = compute_mauve(p_text=p_text, q_text=q_text,
                    device_id=0,           # use GPU 0 for featurization
                    max_text_length=256)   # truncate text to 256 tokens
print('MAUVE(P,Q) =', out.mauve)
```

FIGURES
- Best candidate: Figure 1, p.2. "MAUVE compares the machine text distribution Q to that of human text P by using the family of mixtures Rλ = λP+(1−λ)Q... Illustration of Type I errors, where Q produces degenerate, repetitive text... and, Type II errors, where Q cannot produce plausible human text." The panel pairs a repetitive "the time is the time is" example with a rare place-name sentence, so the two error types are clear at a glance.
- Alternative: Figure 2, p.3, which shows actual divergence curves with MAUVE as the shaded area.
- Alternative: Figure 4, p.7, which shows MAUVE against Fréchet distance, Gen. PPL and sparsemax as generations get longer.

FIT WITH THE NOTES
- Best fit: generative-ai/08-eval/notes/12-failure-modes.md, the "Overlap metrics on open-ended text" bullet (line 228). The paper supports what that bullet says. It states that n-gram reference metrics are "fundamentally ill-suited for open-ended generation" and weakly agree with humans (citing Novikova et al. 2017), and it offers the reference-free distributional alternative. Its finding that MAUVE falls with length complements the note's point that ROUGE-L rises with output length. It does not contradict anything there. One caveat if this is cited: MAUVE was never compared against ROUGE/BLEU on references, only against Self-BLEU, Gen. PPL, Zipf, REP and Distinct-4.
- Secondary fit: generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/notes/06-generation-for-rag.md. The ALCE table row (line 310) mentions fluency without naming MAUVE. A short clause could say that ALCE's fluency score is MAUVE, a corpus-level score that cannot judge one answer or check facts. Neither note mentions MAUVE today, so nothing in them is contradicted. The DR-score paragraph at line 405 is a fair contrast, since DR is per answer and reference-based while MAUVE covers the whole corpus with no references. This paper does not discuss ALCE, so the claim that ALCE uses MAUVE has to come from the ALCE paper itself.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Extraction faults:
  - The code listing came out with letters spaced apart.
  - Superscripts were lost: "103 clusters" on p.8 means 10^3, which Appendix C.3 confirms with "1000 components".
  - Subscripted standard deviations run into the main numbers in Tables 6, 8 and 9, e.g. "0 .5890.018" = 0.589 ± 0.018.
- Typos in the paper itself:
  - The order-preservation statement in C.3.1 (p.19) reads "MAUVEc2(P,Q 2) > MAUVEc2(P,Q 2)", where Q1 was meant on one side.
  - The Pareto-frontier formula in A.1 repeats KL(P|R⋆λ) twice.
